It is associated with lower cardiac output in the early postoperative period
It is associated with greater blood loss than hypothermic CPB
It allows safe periods of very low perfusion flow rate or circulatory arrest

explanation.text: With normothermic CPB, **cerebral venous oxygen saturation below 50%** has been observed, particularly during the **early period** of CPB.

head: Hypothermic CPB
Normothermic CPB (possible advantages)

Cerebral venous O~2~ saturation **<50%**, especially early in CPB

explanation.text: CPB is combined with at least some degree of hypothermia in many situations; the possible advantages of normothermic CPB **continue to be explored**.

stem: In a small adult, the surgical situation compels the use of **smaller-than-usual** arterial and venous cannulae. According to the principles of cannula selection, what is an acceptable way to proceed?

choices.text: Keep the full calculated flow, because total perfusion flow is a fixed absolute quantity
Raise the arterial line pressure above 300 mmHg to deliver the full flow
Set the perfusion flow rate at a smaller value or use assisted venous return (vacuum or centrifugal pump)
Choose cannula size by the planned body temperature rather than by flow rate
Use a bubble oxygenator, which lowers resistance in the circuit

explanation.text: Flow is a **range**, not a fixed number: with smaller cannulae, **lower the flow** or add **assisted venous return** (vacuum, centrifugal pump).

steps.text: Cannula size depends on **perfusion flow rate** + **type of venous return**

steps.label: but
steps.text: Total flow (even at normothermia) is a **range of acceptable values**

steps.label: so, if small cannulae are compelled

explanation.title: Do not force flow through a small cannula
explanation.text: A properly positioned cannula of **adequate size** ensures proper arterial line pressure; above 250 to 300 mmHg the risk of line disruption and cavitation rises.
Thus, if the surgical situation compels use of smaller cannulae, perfusion flow rate can be set at a smaller value, or assisted venous return (vacuum, centrifugal pump) can be used.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 64

choiceNotes.a: Total perfusion flow rate, even at normothermia, is **not an absolute quantity** but a range of acceptable values.
choiceNotes.b: Above 250 to 300 mmHg, the risk of **arterial line disruption and cavitation** at the arterial cannula increases.
choiceNotes.d: Cannula size is determined primarily by **perfusion flow rate and type of venous return**.
choiceNotes.e: **Microporous and true membrane** oxygenators have advantages over bubble oxygenators and are the ones currently indicated; the remedy for small cannulae is lower flow or assisted venous return.

stem: During mitral valve surgery with a single **two-stage venous cannula** inserted through the right atrial appendage, venous return falls each time the surgeon retracts strongly for exposure. What is the best explanation?

Marked retraction for exposure can partially obstruct drainage through a single two-stage cannula
A two-stage cannula decompresses the right heart poorly, so it is unsuitable for mitral surgery
Retraction compresses the side holes, which normally lie in the IVC below the diaphragm
An air lock forms because air enters the right atrium through the tricuspid valve

explanation.text: **Marked retraction** for exposure, as in **mitral valve surgery**, can **partially obstruct** drainage through a two-stage single venous cannula.

children: Aortic valve, mitral valve, ascending aorta
**Marked retraction** (e.g., mitral surgery) can partially obstruct drainage

explanation.title: Two cannulae instead
explanation.text: Two venous cannulae may be used routinely or primarily for congenital operations (including infants) and operations involving the **right atrium**, such as tricuspid valve surgery.

stem: A patient is being positioned for a median sternotomy. Which positioning measure is recommended?

choices.text: The trunk rotated slightly toward the left to improve exposure of the heart
In infants, a pad placed under the neck so that the head is flexed forward
Temperature probes placed in the esophagus and the rectum
Arms at the side, secured and protected against ulnar nerve compression
External defibrillation pads placed on the right chest and the abdomen

explanation.text: Arms at the side avoid **traction on the brachial plexus**; they must be **secured and protected** so the **ulnar nerve** is not compressed at the elbow.

items: Both arms at the side (or a carefully positioned **arm board for the left arm**)
Infants: **pad under the back** → chest forward, neck extended
Trunk **not rotated**
Cautery pad under the buttocks or back; defibrillation pads on the **anterolateral left chest and back**
Thermistors: **bladder** (urethral catheter) and **nasopharynx**

explanation.title: Why it matters
explanation.text: An improperly positioned patient can make the operation more difficult **and injure the patient**; the surgeon positions the patient together with the anesthesiologist.
The patient’s trunk must not be rotated, and the arms at the side must be secured and protected to prevent compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 65

choiceNotes.a: The patient's trunk **must not be rotated**.
choiceNotes.b: In infants, the pad goes **under the back** to project the chest forward and **extend** the neck.
choiceNotes.c: The source places a **thermistor urethral catheter in the bladder** and a **thermistor probe in the nasopharynx**.
choiceNotes.e: Defibrillation pads may be placed on the **anterolateral left chest and the back**.

stem: While the surgeon divides the sternum with the saw during a primary median sternotomy, what should the anesthesiologist do?

choices.text: Hyperinflate the lungs to hold the pleura against the sternum
Continue normal ventilation, because the pleura is rarely entered
Give the full heparin dose so that cannulation can follow at once
Tilt the table head-down so the heart falls away from the sternum
Stop ventilating the patient and exert no pressure on the lungs

explanation.text: During sawing, ventilation **stops** and **no pressure** is put on the lungs, so the **soft tissue and pleura fall away** from the sternum.

items: Blade held snugly against the **posterior** surface of the manubrium; toe of the saw kept **hugging the back** of the sternum
Stay precisely in the **midline**: drifting makes the sternum spread unevenly and closure harder
Alternative: divide **from the bottom up**; in neonates and infants, scissors may be used after excising the xiphoid

explanation.title: Midline matters
explanation.text: Drifting away from the midline must be avoided: the sternum will not spread evenly and its later closure will be more difficult.
During sawing, the anesthesiologist should cease ventilating the patient and exert no pressure on the lungs so that the soft tissue and pleura will fall away from the sternum.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 65

choiceNotes.a: The lungs must **not** be pressurized; the aim is for the soft tissue and pleura to **fall away** from the sternum.
choiceNotes.b: Ventilation must **cease** during sawing so the pleura falls away from the sternum; infrequent pleural entry depends on a properly made incision.
choiceNotes.c: A baseline ACT is established **after** sternotomy, and heparin is given afterward.
choiceNotes.d: Head-down tilt is a **de-airing** step at the end of the repair, not a sternotomy step.

stem: After a median sternotomy, the sternal retractor is opened widely, particularly at the upper half of the sternum. Which complication is specifically attributed to this **excessive retraction**?

Compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow
Entry into the peritoneal cavity at the diaphragm
Expanding hematoma from the remaining thymus
Uneven sternal spreading with difficult later closure

explanation.text: Opening the retractor more than necessary, especially at the **upper half** of the sternum, may injure the **brachial plexus** and damage the **stellate ganglion**.

explanation.title: How to open

choiceNotes.b: Ulnar nerve compression is prevented by **securing and protecting the arms** at the side during positioning.

stem: For routine ascending aortic cannulation in an adult with a normal **left** aortic arch, where should the purse-string sutures be sited?

choices.text: Outside (downstream of) the pericardial reflection, where the aortic wall is tougher
Within the pericardial reflection, a little to the right side of the anterior aortic surface
Within the pericardial reflection, a little to the left side of the anterior aortic surface
At or beyond the orifice of the brachiocephalic artery in every patient
At the site of the cardioplegic needle, so that one purse string serves both

explanation.text: Cannulate **within the pericardial reflection** (tougher aorta, upstream of the brachiocephalic artery), a little **to the left** of the anterior surface.

Reason

Main role in this section

Cannulate the femoral vein, since peripheral cannulation suits very small patients
Proceed to circulatory arrest without venous cannulation
Keep retracting the heart and accept brief hypotension until the IVC cannula is in
Cannulate the SVC first, start partial CPB, then expose and cannulate the IVC

explanation.text: When IVC exposure is difficult, **cannulate the SVC first**, start **partial CPB**, and **then** expose and cannulate the IVC.

steps.text: Large heart in a neonate or infant
Then IVC tape, purse string, and cannula

explanation.title: How low in weight?
explanation.text: Two venous cannulae inserted directly into the cavae are well suited for children, infants, and neonates down to about **2.5 kg**; drainage can be verified by **SVC pressure** from a small internal jugular catheter.

When exposure of the IVC is particularly difficult, the SVC may be cannulated first, partial CPB established, and the IVC then exposed for placing the tape and purse-string suture and for inserting the cannula.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 68

choiceNotes.a: The source cannulates the **SVC first**, because exposing the IVC is the difficult, hypotension-provoking step.
choiceNotes.b: In **very small patients**, peripheral cannulation is **not practical**.
choiceNotes.c: The source's solution is **SVC cannulation and partial CPB**, after which the IVC is exposed.
choiceNotes.d: These exposure maneuvers can lead to **severe** hypotension; the source avoids them by starting partial CPB first.

stem: After direct cannulation of both venae cavae for an intracardiac repair, how must the cannula tips lie to avoid **venous obstruction**?

choices.text: Both tips pointing toward the right atrium to collect atrial blood
Parallel to the caval walls; SVC tip upward, IVC tip downward
Perpendicular to the caval walls to maximize the inflow area
SVC tip pointing downward and IVC tip pointing upward
Both tips crossed in the mid-right atrium

choiceNotes.c: Each tip must lie **directly parallel** to the walls of the vena cava.
choiceNotes.d: This is the reverse of the recommended orientation.
choiceNotes.e: Mid-right atrial **side holes** belong to the single two-stage cannula, not to direct caval cannulae.

stem: A neonate is placed on CPB with a **cold prime** (18°C to 22°C). What should the team anticipate as bypass begins?

choices.text: The heart's contribution to total flow rises, so pump flow can be increased slowly
Myocardial function is unaffected until the nasopharyngeal temperature falls below 25°C
Heart rate rises and contraction becomes more vigorous for several minutes
Heart rate slows and contraction is impaired, so the arterial pump must reach full flow rapidly
Ventricular distention cannot occur because the cold heart is stiff

explanation.text: A **cold prime** immediately slows and weakens the heart, so its share of flow falls fast: the **arterial pump must reach full flow rapidly**.

steps.text: Heart's contribution to total flow **rapidly diminishes**
Arterial pump must **rapidly reach full flow**

explanation.title: Watch the ventricle
explanation.text: Neonates and infants have **high ventricular compliance** and a heart **less tolerant of excessive preload**; watch for distention.
If a cold prime is used, myocardial function is immediately affected after establishing CPB. Heart rate slows, and contraction is impaired.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.a: With a cold prime the heart's contribution **rapidly diminishes**, so the pump must reach full flow **rapidly**.
choiceNotes.b: Myocardial function is affected **immediately** after establishing CPB with a cold prime.
choiceNotes.c: Heart rate **slows** and contraction is **impaired**.
choiceNotes.e: The heart must be watched for **ventricular distention**, especially in infants and neonates with high ventricular compliance.

stem: Shortly after CPB is commenced in an infant, the heart is seen to become **distended**. What should be done?

choices.text: Reduce pump flow and reposition the venous cannulae
Increase pump flow to unload the ventricle
Raise venous pressure by reducing venous drainage
Stop ventilation at once, whatever the cardiac contractility
Add cold prime to slow the heart further

explanation.text: Distention on initiation → **reduce pump flow** and **reposition the venous cannulae**.

explanation.title: Why infants are at risk
explanation.text: Infants and neonates have **high ventricular compliance** and a heart **less tolerant of excessive preload**.
If distention occurs, pump flow must be reduced and the venous cannulae repositioned.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.b: If distention occurs, pump flow must be **reduced**, not increased.
choiceNotes.c: Reducing venous drainage to fill the heart is a step for **inserting a left heart vent** in a beating heart; it would worsen distention.
choiceNotes.d: If contractility is maintained, it is preferable to **maintain ventilation** until full flow is achieved.
choiceNotes.e: Cold prime impairs contraction; the remedy for distention is **lower flow and venous cannula repositioning**.

stem: In an adult, a left-heart vent is to be inserted through a purse string at the junction of the right superior pulmonary vein and left atrium while the heart is **beating** and the aorta is **not clamped**. Which maneuver reduces the risk of cerebral air embolism?

choices.text: Increase venous pressure by reducing venous drainage, so the heart fills with blood
Maximize venous drainage to empty the heart before the incision
Insert the vent through the pulmonary trunk, which decompresses best
Advance the catheter blindly, without palpating its tip
Make the purse string large enough to encircle the pulmonary vein orifice

explanation.text: Before opening the left atrium of a beating heart, **reduce venous drainage** so venous pressure and cardiac blood volume **rise**; air then cannot easily enter and embolize.

steps.text: Purse string: atrial wall + pulmonary vein adventitia (orifice spared)
Palpate tip from behind the heart → through **mitral valve** into LV

explanation.title: Left heart vent via right superior pulmonary vein
Same risk on the way out
explanation.text: The same precautions against air are needed when the vent is **withdrawn** at the end of the operation.
This must be done precisely if the heart is beating because air can be introduced into it and embolize to the brain unless the aorta has been clamped.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.b: An empty beating heart can draw in air; the source **reduces** venous drainage to increase blood volume in the heart.
choiceNotes.c: With the pulmonary trunk, drainage and decompression of the left heart **may be suboptimal**.
choiceNotes.d: The left hand is placed **behind the heart** to palpate the tip and guide it through the mitral valve.
choiceNotes.e: The stitch **should not** be large enough to compromise the pulmonary vein orifice when tied.

stem: For tricuspid valve surgery with two caval cannulae, the right atrium is opened. The atrial septum is **intact** (no PFO or ASD), and the left heart is to be vented with a sump catheter placed across the septum. Where is the stab wound made?

choices.text: In the fossa ovalis, directly beneath the superior limbus
In the coronary sinus ostium
In the inferior fossa ovalis, close to the IVC orifice
Anywhere along the interatrial groove
Through the anterior limbus near the aortic root

explanation.text: Without a PFO or ASD, stab the **fossa ovalis directly beneath the superior limbus**; otherwise the vent may end up **outside the heart**.

branches.label: neither
branches.text: Stab wound in fossa ovalis **beneath the superior limbus**

explanation.title: A two-chamber sump
explanation.text: Because the sump lies only **partially across** the septum, it removes **both left and right atrial blood**; the right atrium stays open during the repair.

If neither is present, a stab wound is made in the fossa ovalis directly beneath the superior limbus. If this landmark is not used and the stab wound is imprecisely made, the vent may come to lie outside the heart
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.b: The coronary sinus ostium is a site for picking up **left SVC** flow, not for entering the left atrium.
choiceNotes.c: The landmark is the **superior limbus**; an imprecise stab wound may place the vent **outside the heart**.
choiceNotes.d: An imprecisely made stab wound may leave the vent **outside the heart** rather than in the left atrium.
choiceNotes.e: The stab wound is made **directly beneath the superior limbus**, in the fossa ovalis.

stem: Rewarming is begun after most of the repair is complete. Which set of temperature targets is recommended?

choices.text: Water 45°C; arterial blood not above 41°C; nasopharynx at 37°C when stopping CPB
Water 42°C; arterial blood up to 42°C; nasopharynx at 35°C when stopping CPB
Water 39°C; arterial blood not above 37°C; nasopharynx at 34°C when stopping CPB
Water 42°C; arterial blood not above 39°C; nasopharynx at 37°C for about 10 minutes before stopping CPB
Water 42°C; arterial blood not above 39°C; stop CPB as soon as the nasopharynx reaches 34°C

explanation.text: Rewarm with water at **42°C**, keep arterial blood **≤39°C**, and hold the nasopharynx at **37°C for about 10 minutes** before stopping CPB.

explanation.title: Why wait 10 minutes?
explanation.text: To avoid **excessive downward temperature drift** in the postbypass period; this is advantageous but not essential.
For rewarming, the water in the heat exchanger is raised to 42°C; the arterial blood temperature should not exceed 39°C.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.a: The heat-exchanger water is raised to **42°C**, and arterial blood should **not exceed 39°C**.
choiceNotes.b: Arterial blood should not exceed **39°C**, and the nasopharyngeal target before stopping is **37°C**.
choiceNotes.c: Water is raised to **42°C**; the nasopharynx should reach **37°C**.
choiceNotes.e: It is advantageous to hold the nasopharynx at **37°C for about 10 minutes** before stopping, to avoid downward temperature drift.

stem: As the cardiac chambers are being closed after an open-heart repair, the team prepares to de-air the heart. Which is one of the **established principles** of de-airing?

choices.text: Keep the lungs deflated throughout so that no air is pushed into the heart
Allow the heart to eject first, then aspirate any remaining air
Stop aortic vent suction as soon as the heart begins to eject
Keep the heart arrested and empty while air is removed
Fill the heart with blood or electrolyte solution before closing it

explanation.text: Principle 1 of de-airing: **fill the heart with fluid** (blood or electrolyte solution) **before closing** it, to minimize air entrapment.

items: **Fill** the heart with fluid before closing
Heart **reperfused and beating**
**Aspirate** residual air **before** the heart ejects
**Intermittently ventilate** the lungs to express air from the pulmonary veins
**Continuous suction** on an ascending aortic needle vent (or a freely bleeding stab wound) as ejection begins

explanation.title: Why it matters
explanation.text: Clinical studies show a **correlation between the number of gaseous microemboli and the severity of neuropsychological impairment** after CPB.
The heart is filled with fluid (blood or electrolyte solution) before closing to minimize air entrapment.

choiceNotes.a: The lungs are **intermittently ventilated** to express air from the pulmonary veins.
choiceNotes.b: Residual air is aspirated **before** allowing the heart to eject.
choiceNotes.c: **Continuous suction** is applied on the aortic needle vent as the heart commences ejecting.
choiceNotes.d: The heart must be **reperfused and beating**, and filled with fluid.

stem: During de-airing at the end of an **aortic valve replacement**, which step follows the technique described?

choices.text: Inflate the lungs vigorously while the aortotomy is still open
Needle-aspirate the LV through the front of its apex
Tilt the table head-up before slowly releasing the aortic clamp
Raise perfusion flow as the aortic clamp is released
Remove the aortic needle vent as soon as the heart starts to eject

explanation.text: Needle aspiration through the **front of the LV apex** removes the air pocket that is **almost always present** there.

steps.text: Fill heart; inject fluid if blood does not escape from the aortotomy; **gentle** lung inflation
Aspirate the **LA dome**; invert the LA appendage
Aspirate the **LV apex** (heart pulled forward and to the right)
Release clamp slowly with **reduced flow**; aspirate the aortic needle vent
Remove LA vent, defibrillate if needed, shake the LV; heart ejects as CVP rises to 10 mmHg
Level the table; remove the aortic vent **last**

explanation.title: Do not hurry
explanation.text: These maneuvers should not be hurried; the aortic needle vent should not be removed until the heart has been ejecting well **for some time**.
This is a simple and effective way of removing the pocket of air that is almost always present at this site.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 70

choiceNotes.a: Inflation must be **gentle**: when the lungs collapse, air can be drawn into the LV through the **still-opened aorta**.
choiceNotes.c: The table is tilted with the patient's **head down**.
choiceNotes.d: Perfusion flow is **temporarily reduced** as the clamp is slowly released, and LV overdistention must be prevented.
choiceNotes.e: The **longer** the aortic needle vent is in use, the better; it stays until the heart has been ejecting well for some time.

stem: After CPB through a median sternotomy, the pericardium is generally left open. What is an advantage of this practice?

choices.text: It completely eliminates the risk of tamponade
It reduces the tendency of retained blood to create positive intrapericardial pressure
It allows the mediastinal drainage tubes to be omitted
It lets blood collect around the heart to tamponade suture-line bleeding
It is used only when the aorta or an aortic graft is prominent

explanation.text: An open pericardium **drains** mediastinal and substernal blood and **reduces** (not eliminates) the risk of **tamponade**.

items: **Good blood drainage** from mediastinal and substernal tissues into the pericardium (then out through the tubes) → **no hematomas** there
**Less positive intrapericardial pressure** from retained blood → less **tamponade**

explanation.title: Reoperation
explanation.text: Reoperations have **not posed a major problem** with this technique; a few sutures may cover a prominent aorta or aortic graft.
reduction (but not elimination) of the tendency of retained blood to produce a positive intrapericardial pressure
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: The tendency to positive intrapericardial pressure is **reduced, but not eliminated**.
choiceNotes.c: Blood drains into the pericardial cavity **and then out through the drainage tubes**.
choiceNotes.d: The advantage is **good drainage** that prevents hematomas, not retention of blood.
choiceNotes.e: A prominent aorta or graft is the situation where a **few sutures** may be placed at the upper end.

explanation.text: Thin or fragmented edges: **vertical parasternal wires** in front of and behind the **costal cartilages**, then incorporated into the **transverse** wires.

Wires are **twisted, not tied**
**Sternal plating** may replace or supplement cerclage wires
Absorbable sutures for muscles and linea alba; skin subcuticular or staples

explanation.title: Fragile sternum
explanation.text: In older patients with a fragile sternum, **avoid bone wax** altogether.
If the sternal edges are thin or fragmented, wire sutures can be passed vertically in the parasternal position in front of and behind the costal cartilages on one or both sides.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: Stainless steel wires are **twisted, not tied**.
choiceNotes.b: Absorbable sutures close the **muscles and linea alba**; the sternum is closed with stainless steel wire (or plates).
choiceNotes.c: When the sternum is fragile, as in older patients, it is better to **avoid wax altogether**.
choiceNotes.d: Leaving the sternum open is for a **suboptimal hemodynamic state**, not for fragile bone.

stem: After a long operation, the patient's hemodynamic state is **suboptimal** as preparations are made to close the chest. What does the source recommend?

choices.text: Close the sternum and support the heart with inotropes, as an open chest rarely helps
Leave the chest unsutured and plan secondary closure in 24 to 48 hours
Leave the sternum open but close the skin over it
Leave the sternum open and plan secondary closure after 7 to 10 days
Leave the sternum open, preferably covered by a sutured silicone rubber sheet

explanation.text: With a **suboptimal hemodynamic state**, leave the chest **open** (sternum, subcutaneous tissue, skin) and close it **24 to 48 hours** later.

steps.label: instead
steps.text: Leave unsutured; **vacuum-assisted** wound care (or loose packing + adhesive sheet)

explanation.title: Lifesaving
explanation.text: This maneuver, regardless of technical details, is **lifesaving** in some patients.
Vacuum-assisted wound care systems have largely replaced the use of an impervious sheet of silicone rubber or bovine pericardium to temporarily cover the mediastinal structures.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: Closing the sternum **frequently further depresses cardiac function**; leaving it open is **lifesaving** in some patients.
choiceNotes.c: The sternum, subcutaneous tissue, **and skin** are all left unsutured.
choiceNotes.d: Secondary closure can usually be performed **24 to 48 hours** later.
choiceNotes.e: **Vacuum-assisted wound care** systems have largely replaced silicone rubber or bovine pericardium sheets.

stem: Which statement about the components of the pump-oxygenator is correct?

choices.text: Venous reservoirs substantially reduce the priming volume of the system
The oxygenator is the least damaging part of the extracorporeal apparatus
Bubble oxygenators are currently indicated for cardiac surgery
Integrated heat exchangers are less efficient but reduce priming volume
Priming volume should be cut by removing every possible component

explanation.text: **Integrated** heat exchangers: **less efficient** than freestanding ones, but **lower priming volume**.

head: Component
Key point
rows: Lets **air escape** and **stores** excess volume (hard-shell type allows VAVR); **increases** priming volume
Most varied, most important, probably **most damaging**; microporous or true membrane
Integrated = **less efficient**, **less priming volume**; freestanding = more efficient
Roller pump set **slightly nonocclusive**, calibrated often; or centrifugal with ultrasonic flow measurement
explanation.caption: Pump-oxygenator components

explanation.title: Priming volume trade-off
explanation.text: Every component adds priming volume, but **oversimplifying** the system can compromise safety.
Integrated heat exchangers are generally less efficient than freestanding ones, but they reduce priming volume.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: Venous reservoirs, although useful, **substantially increase** priming volume.
choiceNotes.b: The oxygenator is probably the **most damaging** part of the apparatus (and the most important).
choiceNotes.c: **Microporous and true membrane** oxygenators have advantages over bubble oxygenators and are currently indicated.
choiceNotes.e: Systems can be so **oversimplified** to reduce priming volume that **safety may be compromised**.

stem: During CPB, the arterial line pressure in the pump-oxygenator rises to **320 mmHg**. What is the main concern?

choices.text: None; pressures up to 400 mmHg are acceptable with a roller pump
It suggests the arterial cannula is too large for the aorta
It indicates an air lock in the venous line
It shows the roller pump is slightly nonocclusive and should be made fully occlusive
Increased risk of arterial line disruption and of cavitation near the arterial cannula

explanation.text: Arterial line pressure **above 250 to 300 mmHg** increases the risk of **line disruption** and **cavitation** at the arterial cannula.

explanation.title: Arterial pump set-up
explanation.text: Roller pump: adjusted to be **slightly nonocclusive** and **calibrated** often so flow is accurate. Centrifugal pump: use **ultrasonic flow measurement**.
When this pressure exceeds 250 to 300 mmHg, risk of disruption of the arterial line and cavitation in the region of the arterial cannula increases.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: Risk rises when arterial line pressure **exceeds 250 to 300 mmHg**.
choiceNotes.b: The source links proper arterial line pressure to a properly positioned cannula of **adequate size**; it does not describe a too-large cannula as the cause.
choiceNotes.c: An air lock stops **venous return** to the pump; it is not an arterial line pressure problem.
choiceNotes.d: The roller pump **should** be adjusted to be **slightly nonocclusive** before each perfusion.

stem: Which statement about a **low-porosity (40-µm) filter** in the arterial line is supported?

choices.text: A randomized CABG study showed better neuropsychiatric function only with the filter
Gaseous microemboli are more prevalent with membrane than with bubble oxygenators
It considerably reduces gaseous microemboli on transcranial Doppler studies
It is unnecessary with membrane oxygenators, which produce no gaseous microemboli
One filter type should be used everywhere, regardless of the other circuit components

explanation.text: 40-µm arterial filters **considerably reduce gaseous microemboli** on transcranial Doppler; **routine use appears beneficial**.

head: Evidence
Finding
rows: Good neuropsychiatric function **with or without** filter
explanation.caption: Arterial line filter

explanation.title: Still somewhat controversial
explanation.text: Advantages, disadvantages, and need for the filter remain **somewhat controversial**; the exact filter is chosen **within each institution**.
Currently, routine use of a low-porosity filter of this type in the arterial line appears to be beneficial.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: Walker's randomized study showed **good** neuropsychiatric function **whether or not** a filter was present.
choiceNotes.b: Gaseous microemboli are **more prevalent with bubble** oxygenators.
choiceNotes.d: Microemboli are **less prevalent** (not absent) with membrane oxygenators, and routine filter use appears beneficial.
choiceNotes.e: The exact filter and its compatibility with other components must be **determined within each institution**.

stem: Which statement about **cardiotomy suction** in the CPB circuit is correct?

choices.text: Aspirated blood can return to the circuit without filtration or defoaming
Blood may be left in the pericardium to reduce suction trauma
Blocking the open end of a roller-pump sucker rapidly raises suction
One cardiotomy suction port is generally sufficient
A rapidly variable high-capacity vacuum system is the current standard

explanation.text: Roller-pump suckers: when the open end is **blocked, suction rises rapidly** and may damage **tissue or blood**, so **constant monitoring** is needed.

items: **At least two** cardiotomy suction ports
Blood passes a **low-porosity filter** and is **defoamed** in a separate chamber open to air
Aspirate pericardial blood **promptly** (stagnant blood can promote thrombolysis)
Ideal: variable high-capacity vacuum; in practice: **roller pumps** with constant monitoring

explanation.text: With this system, when the open end of the line is blocked, the suction rapidly increases; this may damage either the tissue or the blood.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.a: This blood may contain particulate matter and air; it must pass a **low-porosity filter** and be **defoamed** before return.
choiceNotes.b: Blood left too long in the pericardium before being aspirated can **promote thrombolysis**; aspirate promptly.
choiceNotes.d: The circuit should generally contain **at least two** cardiotomy suction ports.
choiceNotes.e: Such a vacuum system would be ideal but has proved **impractical**, so **roller pumps** are used.

stem: A **miniaturized extracorporeal circuit (MECC)** is chosen for CABG. Which feature defines this circuit?

choices.text: Closed and heparin-coated, with only a centrifugal pump and membrane oxygenator
A hard-shell venous reservoir that allows vacuum-assisted venous return
An integral cardiotomy suction device returning shed blood
A roller pump with a microporous oxygenator, open to air
A bubble oxygenator chosen to minimize the priming volume

explanation.text: MECC = **closed**, **heparin-coated** circuit: **centrifugal pump + membrane oxygenator** only; **no venous reservoir**, **no cardiotomy suction**.
These closed circuits with little or no blood/air contact have a controlled vortex (centrifugal) blood pump and a membrane oxygenator as the only components.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.b: MECC has **no venous reservoir**.
choiceNotes.c: MECC has **no integral cardiac suction device**.
choiceNotes.d: MECC circuits are **closed** with little or no blood/air contact and use a **centrifugal** pump.
choiceNotes.e: The oxygenator in MECC is a **membrane** oxygenator.

stem: A meta-analysis of randomized trials compared conventional CPB with **miniaturized CPB circuits** (mostly CABG patients). Which result was found?

choices.text: Lower early mortality, with no difference in the number of transfused patients
More neurologic events, offset by fewer patients needing transfusion
Fewer neurologic events, transfusions, and troponin; same early mortality
No difference in any of the outcomes examined
Fewer neurologic events and lower mortality, but higher troponin

explanation.text: Miniaturized circuits: **fewer neurologic events**, **fewer transfused patients**, **lower peak troponin**; **early mortality unchanged**.

explanation.title: Nonrandomized CABG data also suggest
explanation.text: Fewer transfusions, less troponin release, **less postoperative atrial fibrillation**, **less acute kidney injury**, less thrombin generation, and lower IL-6 and SC5b-9.

miniaturized circuits are associated with substantial reductions in neurologic injury, number of patients requiring transfusion of blood products, and peak cardiac troponin release (Table 2.6). No difference in early mortality was noted.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.a: **No difference in early mortality** was noted; the number of transfused patients was **reduced**.
choiceNotes.b: Neurologic injury was **substantially reduced** with miniaturized circuits.
choiceNotes.d: Neurologic events, transfused patients, and peak troponin were **all reduced**.
choiceNotes.e: Peak troponin was **lower**, and mortality was **not different**.

stem: During a repair **inside the right ventricle** using a single venous cannula without assisted venous return, venous return to the pump suddenly stops and blood floods the right heart. What should be done?

choices.text: Maintain perfusion flow and keep the intracardiac sucker outside the heart
Reduce the perfusion flow rate until venous return recovers
Place the intracardiac sucker deep in the ventricle to aspirate the air
Withdraw the cannula tip from the IVC into the mid-right atrium
Stop the pump until the right heart empties spontaneously

explanation.text: Air lock: **do not reduce perfusion flow**; keep the **sucker outside the heart** to control the pericardial well while the air lock is moved down into the **venous reservoir**.

steps.text: Operation in RV or pulmonary trunk, single cannula, no assisted venous return

steps.label: air enters RA via tricuspid valve

steps.text: Venous return stops abruptly; blood floods the right heart

steps.label: response
steps.text: Flow **unchanged**; sucker **outside** the heart; air lock expelled into the reservoir

explanation.title: When a single cannula is ideal
explanation.text: A single two-stage cannula is optimal for many adult operations and in neonates, infants, and children when the **entire repair** is done during **hypothermic circulatory arrest**.
The perfusionist must not reduce the perfusion flow rate, but instead, the intracardiac sucker is positioned outside the heart to keep blood from overflowing from the pericardial well
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.b: The perfusionist **must not reduce** the perfusion flow rate.
choiceNotes.c: The sucker is positioned **outside the heart** to keep blood from overflowing the pericardial well.
choiceNotes.d: The principle remains: **tip in the IVC**, side holes in the right atrium.
choiceNotes.e: Flow is maintained while the air lock is **moved down the venous line** and expelled into the venous reservoir.

stem: A patient with a severely atheromatous aorta needs arch surgery with antegrade cerebral perfusion. Axillary cannulation is planned, but there is atheroma at the **orifice of the brachiocephalic artery**. Which risk and strategy are described?

choices.text: No embolic risk, because axillary perfusion is antegrade; proceed routinely
Change to femoral cannulation, because retrograde perfusion carries no embolic risk
Begin full systemic perfusion first, then isolate the arch vessels
Atheroemboli from that lesion; start cerebral perfusion before systemic perfusion
Cannulate the ascending aorta instead, since antegrade aortic perfusion is always feasible

explanation.text: Axillary flow can dislodge atheroma at the **brachiocephalic orifice**; isolate the **arch vessels early** with cerebral perfusion **before systemic perfusion**.

steps.label: Shiiya
steps.text: ACP from **right and left axillary** arteries + **direct left common carotid** perfusion

head: Route
Embolic concern
rows: Preferred, but atheroma may preclude it
Emboli from atheroma at the **brachiocephalic orifice**
explanation.caption: Arterial routes in the atheromatous patient

explanation.text: Axillary arterial cannulation became a popular strategy; however, it is possible to cause atheroemboli from an atheromatous lesion at the orifice of the brachiocephalic artery.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 73

choiceNotes.a: Axillary cannulation **can** cause atheroemboli from an atheromatous lesion at the brachiocephalic orifice.
choiceNotes.b: **Retrograde embolization** by debris from femoral cannulation is a well-recognized phenomenon.
choiceNotes.c: Shiiya's approach starts cerebral perfusion **before** initiating systemic perfusion.
choiceNotes.e: An atheromatous aorta **sometimes precludes** ascending aortic cannulation.

stem: For a high-risk **reoperation**, CPB is established through the groin before the sternum is reopened. The **left** femoral vein must be used for venous drainage. What is the recommended technique?

choices.text: Advance a short cannula only as far as the iliac vein
Use a small (16F) cannula to limit injury to the vein
Insert the cannula without a guidewire, as is usual from the left side
Expose the vein above the inguinal ligament through a lower abdominal incision
Pass the cannula over a guidewire placed into the right atrium or IVC

explanation.text: From the **left** femoral vein, a **guidewire** (tip in the right atrium or adjacent IVC) is often needed to pass the long cannula **over the sacral promontory into the IVC**.

head: Open technique
Seldinger technique
rows: Vertical or oblique groin-crease incision; below the inguinal ligament
Appropriate size, transverse arteriotomy between clamps
Large **28F to 32F**, long, into the IVC
Guidewire often needed from the left side
explanation.caption: Femoral cannulation

explanation.title: Why go peripheral first?
explanation.text: To establish CPB **before opening the sternum** in reoperations with a high probability of entering a cardiac chamber or major artery during sternotomy.

If the left femoral vein is used, it is often necessary to insert a guidewire, positioning the tip in the right atrium or the adjacent IVC, and then the venous cannula, which is inserted over the wire.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 73

choiceNotes.a: A large, **long** cannula must be advanced **over the sacral promontory into the IVC**.
choiceNotes.b: A **large (28F to 32F)** long cannula is used with open femoral cannulation.
choiceNotes.c: From the **right** femoral vein this is usually easy; from the **left** a guidewire is often necessary.
choiceNotes.d: A groin-crease incision is used, working **inferiorly** from the inguinal ligament to the common femoral vessels.

stem: A patient with an existing **aortic dissection** needs peripheral arterial cannulation, and the axillary artery is chosen instead of the femoral artery. Which is a listed advantage of axillary cannulation?

choices.text: Proximal and distal control of the artery is not needed
Brain blood flow during otherwise whole-body circulatory arrest
Exposure carries no risk to the brachial plexus
Cannulation can be performed without systemic heparin
It needs no incision because it is always done percutaneously

explanation.text: Axillary cannulation avoids **malperfusion**, maintains **brain blood flow** during otherwise whole-body circulatory arrest, and presumably avoids **retrograde particulate embolization**.

steps.text: Transverse incision **below the lateral two-thirds** of the clavicle
Split **pectoralis major** along its fibers; incise clavipectoral fascia
Free the artery, **sparing the brachial plexus**
Heparin; cannulate directly or via an **8- or 10-mm graft** sewn end to side

explanation.text: Advantages include absence of malperfusion, establishment of brain blood flow during otherwise whole-body circulatory arrest, and presumably lack of retrograde particulate embolization.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 73

choiceNotes.a: **Proximal and distal control** of the axillary artery is obtained before cannulation.
choiceNotes.c: Dissection must take care **not to injure the branches of the brachial plexus**.
choiceNotes.d: The artery is cannulated **after administration of heparin**.
choiceNotes.e: The artery is exposed through a **transverse incision below the lateral two-thirds of the clavicle**.

stem: A 25-kg child needs a **high-risk redo sternotomy**, and the peripheral vessels are too small for practical cannulation. Which cannulation strategy is described for full CPB before the sternum is opened?

choices.text: Open the sternum first, then cannulate the ascending aorta and right atrium
Brachiocephalic artery above the sternal notch and IVC below the xiphoid
SVC cannulated through the sternal notch and aorta through the xiphoid incision
Ascending aorta cannulated through a right anterolateral thoracotomy
Femoral artery and vein cannulated by the Seldinger technique

explanation.text: Expose the **brachiocephalic artery** just **above the sternal notch** and the **IVC** just **below the xiphoid**, using the **upper and lower poles** of the sternotomy incision.

children: Upper and lower poles of the sternotomy incision
Very small patients where peripheral cannulation is impractical

explanation.title: Other less common arterial sites
explanation.text: Brachial, brachiocephalic, and carotid arteries.
This technique is particularly useful for patients weighing 40 kg or less, in whom these vessels are easily accessible, and in very small patients in whom peripheral cannulation is not practical.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 73

choiceNotes.a: The aim is full CPB support **while** the sternum is opened.
choiceNotes.c: The **artery** cannulated above the sternal notch is the **brachiocephalic** artery; the **IVC** is cannulated below the xiphoid.
choiceNotes.d: Through a right anterolateral thoracotomy, ascending aortic cannulation **may be difficult**; this is not the described strategy.
choiceNotes.e: The described technique is useful in very small patients in whom **peripheral cannulation is not practical**.

choices.text: Peripheral cannulation is limited to reoperative sternotomy

Only the arterial side can be cannulated percutaneously
Percutaneous venous drainage requires cannulae of 32F or larger

Preoperative and postoperative cardiac surgical patients
Support of high-risk patients during percutaneous interventions

explanation.text: In this setting, the pump-oxygenator should be used with a controlled vortex pump or VAVR, which permits use of smaller (22F or 24F) venous cannulae.

choiceNotes.d: A controlled vortex pump or VAVR permits **smaller (22F or 24F)** venous cannulae.
choiceNotes.e: **Resuscitation** of preoperative and postoperative cardiac surgical patients is an indication.

stem: After induction, **700 mL** of blood is removed from an adult with a hematocrit of 40% for later reinfusion. How should this blood be handled?

choices.text: Refrigerated in CPD bags to preserve platelet function, then given after protamine
Kept unrefrigerated and returned into the pump during CPB to limit hemodilution
Kept unrefrigerated and given before protamine, as soon as CPB ends
Sent to the blood bank for washing, then returned the next day
Unrefrigerated in CPD bags, given after protamine and control of bleeding

explanation.text: Prebypass autologous blood: **CPD bags**, **unrefrigerated** in the OR, reinfused **after protamine** and control of major bleeding.

explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 74

choiceNotes.b: This blood is **not used during CPB**; it is given after protamine for its hemostatic and volume effects.

Ultrafiltration keeps plasma proteins; cell salvage loses plasma components
Shed mediastinal blood returned after surgery is rich in clotting factors
Shed mediastinal blood is collected and returned for about 72 hours

What returns
Catch

Plasma components **lost**; heparin in the apparatus

choices.text: Most bleeding comes from surgical sources, so antifibrinolytics are of no value

Tranexamic acid is clearly more effective than epsilon-aminocaproic acid

stem: During bicaval cannulation, a **persistent left SVC** is found. With a pressure needle in the left SVC, the vein is clamped below the needle as a test, and the pressure **rises substantially**. What is the next step?

Insert the additional cannula through the left atrial appendage

stem: In a patient with **heterotaxy**, venous cannulation for CPB is being planned. Which statement about hepatic venous anomalies is correct?

They may join the right or even left atrium independently of the IVC

explanation.text: In heterotaxy, hepatic veins may enter the **right or left atrium independently of the IVC**; the **same options as for a left SVC** apply.

children: Same concerns and options as a left SVC

explanation.text: The hepatic veins may attach to the right atrium or even the left atrium, independent of the IVC attachment. They may attach as a single confluent trunk or as several separate veins.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 74

choiceNotes.a: The hepatic veins may attach to the atria **independently of the IVC attachment**.
choiceNotes.b: They may attach to the right atrium **or even the left atrium**.
choiceNotes.c: They may attach as a single confluent trunk **or as several separate veins**.
choiceNotes.e: A **left SVC** is the most common systemic venous anomaly that influences CPB management.

stem: A young woman with developing breasts is to undergo ASD repair through a **right anterolateral thoracotomy**. Which statement about the set-up is correct?

The patient lies flat, with the right arm abducted above the head

explanation.text: Through a right anterolateral thoracotomy, the pericardium is opened **vertically, 1 to 2 cm anterior and parallel to the phrenic nerve**.

items: **Fourth or fifth** intercostal space; skin incision to the **anterior axillary line**
**Double-lumen** tube; right lung collapsed and retracted posteriorly
Right side **elevated 30 to 40 degrees**; right arm flexed at the side
**Groins draped** into the field

stem: A patient with patent coronary bypass grafts on the ascending aorta needs **redo mitral valve replacement** through a right thoracotomy; the ascending aorta cannot be cannulated or clamped. How is the myocardium managed?

choices.text: Cool to 32°C and defibrillate early, so the heart ejects during the repair
Clamp the ascending aorta through the thoracotomy and give antegrade cardioplegia
Begin rewarming while the left atrium is still open, to shorten bypass time
Hypothermic fibrillation, rewarming only after the left atrium is closed
Avoid any left ventricular suction catheter, to protect the new prosthesis

explanation.text: **Hypothermic fibrillation**: cool until fibrillation (or nasopharynx **18°C to 22°C**), keep the heart **cold and fibrillating**, and **rewarm only after the LA is closed**.

steps.label: cool
steps.text: Heart fibrillates or nasopharynx **18°C to 22°C**; external fibrillator if needed

steps.label: keep
steps.text: **Hypothermic and fibrillating** → no ejection of air into the aorta

steps.label: then
steps.text: **Rewarm**; continuous suction on LV catheter through the mitral valve
Remove catheter just before CPB ends; secure LA suture line

explanation.title: Why not let it beat?
explanation.text: A beating, ejecting heart with an open left side can **eject air into the ascending aorta**.
The heart must be maintained hypothermic and fibrillating to avoid ejection of air into the ascending aorta. Rewarming is not initiated until the left atrium has been closed.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 75

choiceNotes.a: The heart must be **kept hypothermic and fibrillating** to avoid **ejection of air** into the ascending aorta.
choiceNotes.b: In this situation, cannulating and clamping the ascending aorta **may not be possible**.
choiceNotes.c: Rewarming is **not initiated until the left atrium has been closed**.
choiceNotes.e: A soft rubber catheter through the mitral valve or prosthesis is used with **continuous suction during rewarming** to evacuate LV air.
